channel.title: Koshin Studio — Notes (English)
channel.description: Development logs from building browser games and an iOS app, with measured numbers

item.title: Sushi Stack scores stopped reaching the leaderboard: I changed the game’s numbers and forgot the server’s re-check (twice)
item.description: Honest runs of a browser game stopped reaching the online leaderboard: two game values changed without updating the server that re-checks scores. The fix, and a test that compares both sides with the same seeds.

item.title: Japanese Pokémon card & TCG lottery apps compared: Toreca Dash, Toreget, NowPokeca, Pokeka Tracker and Toreca no Chizu
item.description: Five apps and sites that track Pokémon card and TCG lotteries, pre-orders and restocks at stores in Japan, compared on games, alerts, maps and price — by the developer of one of them, weak points included.

item.title: An aggregator crawl read only page 1: card articles were on pages 2–4, and only the first 6,000 characters went to the AI
item.description: The crawl of a stock-information aggregator read only page 1 (mostly consoles), while Pokémon and Gundam articles were on later pages. Only the first 6,000 characters went to the AI, so later stores dropped. I followed 12 pages and read all the text.

item.title: “Not just noticing; not letting it happen”: turning a report-only monitor into one that fills gaps on the spot
item.description: The gap monitor only reported and nothing was filled until a person noticed. I made it create missing articles on the spot, logged a branch that dropped silently, and showed how to apply even with no link. Coverage went from 92% to 100%.

item.title: The same report for the third time: a SwiftUI button responded only on its text, and my two earlier “fixes” did nothing
item.description: The “Won” and “Lost” buttons responded only on the text. Two earlier fixes (modifier order) did not work; I built the look inside a ButtonStyle and replaced six places. A mail-order article with coordinates had the same kind of root.

item.title: “Weird articles keep multiplying”: I counted by creation route and closed the entrances, and my counting was wrong twice
item.description: 252 displayed lotteries were counted by route. Ended rounds left in an aggregator’s table were imported daily with empty deadlines (33); links to search results or top pages and deadlines disagreeing with the store’s own row were closed at the entrance.

item.title: “Automate everything that can be”: counting showed 66 repair jobs had never run on a schedule, and I added only six
item.description: Matching 319 HTTP endpoints against 184 scheduled jobs by call showed 66 that only ran by hand. After a dry run I scheduled only the continuously needed ones, six, and fixed a queue that let the same job pile up.

item.title: “The server went down and I cannot recover it” was wrong: only inbound SSH had been blocked
item.description: From 3:10 a.m. I could not connect to the server and judged it stopped. In fact its processes had run for over 7 days, all 192 scheduled jobs were normal, and only inbound SSH was blocked.

item.title: “ヤマダ電機” versus “ヤマダデンキ”: spelling variants and duplicates had three overlapping causes
item.description: Store names compared only by “contains”, deadlines differing by 59 seconds, and a manual-only dedupe job. I used a general comparison key instead of a synonym table, ran it hourly, and found two dangers in testing.

item.title: “One page = one case” was false: articles of a shop taking 6 products on one form were hidden just for sharing a link
item.description: A job that decided duplicates by link alone hid 5 of 6 articles of a shop taking 6 products on one Google Form. I changed it to link + product. I also found the server’s “entry tiers” were never read by the app.

item.title: English and katakana names share no characters: a fingerprint gate rejected 42 correct matches
item.description: The market-price link rate fell to 39%. The products existed on the market site, but my English names and its katakana names share no characters, so 42 matches were rejected in 26 hours. I kept the gate and added a narrow second judgement for this match only.

item.title: Looking up an ambiguous store name returns Shizuoka, the middle of Japan: I judged by Google’s own answer, not a list of chains
item.description: Passing a store name to Google’s place search with a rectangle covering Japan returned its middle (Shizuoka/Aichi) for ambiguous names. Instead of a list of chain names I judged trust from the answer itself with four rules.

item.title: If you throw failure away, the screen lies: a calendar that said “registered” with none added, a frozen OCR, a notification without a store name
item.description: try? discarded failures, so the calendar showed “registered N events” with 0 added and could never register again, OCR failure froze the screen, and the notification buffer forgot the store name.

item.title: Candidates were found, yet reading the answer failed every time: a URL cut at 200 tokens, and a search that returned 400 on hyphens
item.description: An AI reply choosing an official announcement page was cut at 200 tokens and failed every time. The result stayed 0 because store announcements name no product and the AI obeyed my instruction. Rakuten’s search returned 400 depending on hyphen position.

item.title: A function named “load from iCloud if newer” compared nothing: a 20-record history could become 1
item.description: The iCloud sync function never checked whether data was newer and replaced everything. A fresh device with an empty state could overwrite another device’s 20 records with 1. I added update-time comparison and never overwrite with empty.

item.title: With no ads, 25 real-device checks were blocked: test ads in developer mode only, and no hard-coded prize names
item.description: Before ads were served, 25 of 163 real-device checklist items could not be verified. In developer mode only, the app switches to Google’s test ad units. Prize names are read from one setting and never hard-coded, including in the checklist.

item.title: “That’s just a Beyblade” came back after I added a gate: the blocked value leaked in another form
item.description: A gate “do not create a product whose name contains a toy’s name” was bypassed because the AI’s product name lost the toy’s name. I moved the judgement to the announcement body and rejected only when no card-game word appears.

item.title: Checks that logged “deferred to next run” had never run: three time budgets counted from the same start
item.description: A process had three stages whose time budgets were counted from the same start time, so the rotating 25 checks ran 0 times each run. “Deferred 18 items” meant all of them. I allocated from the job’s time limit and logged each step’s time.

item.title: I fixed a timeout three times and it did not stop: the culprit was a second process under the same lock
item.description: A Rakuten Books stock check timed out 17 times a day. Limiting fetches, then a whole item, did not help; the third time I found that another process under the same lock re-fetched everything with no time limit.

item.title: “It gets cleaned up later” hid an entrance bug: 400 near-identical products were re-created every day
item.description: Catalogue registration looked up existing products by exact name only, so brackets, spaces and full/half-width differences re-created near-identical products daily: 437 in one day, 410 with no articles. The nightly merge job hid it.

item.title: A secret token was in the logs in plain text: scrub at the one exit that cannot be forgotten
item.description: An HTTP library put the request URL in its error message, so a scraping-service token reached the logs. My earlier scrubbing function worked only where called, and there are over 50 callers. I moved the scrubbing to the single exit every log passes through.

item.title: Moving from Cloud Functions to a ¥4,300 server: ¥3,700 a day, Yahoo! failing in the EEA, and five traps
item.description: After the free trial, Cloud Functions cost about ¥3,700 a day because waiting time was billed. I moved almost unchanged code to a Singapore VPS (about ¥4,300 a month). Helsinki failed because Yahoo! blocks the EEA; there were 15 secrets, not 5.

item.title: I opened the links of displayed articles and compared them: about 60 mistakes, and three mistakes in my own first check
item.description: Opening more than 1,000 destination pages and comparing with the articles: Amazon invitation requests shown as first-come, closed or sold-out items displayed, links to other stores or products, application links redirecting to a site’s top page. My first check was wrong in three ways too.

item.title: Four things from a full sweep of 61 audits: 51 jobs clumped at 4 a.m., a lock that expired in 55 seconds, and a price-filling idea I decided not to add
item.description: Once-a-day jobs clumped at 27 at 4 o’clock and 24 at 5; a Rakuten patrol took 181–480 s per run with a 55-second lock; I stopped counting anomalies that cannot be fixed; and I measured a way to fill official prices from one store but did not add it.

item.title: Comparing with other sites to count gaps: the first “23% coverage” was a measuring mistake and the truth was 49%
item.description: Counting whether I show lotteries other sites list: the first 23% was distorted by product-name spelling and expired articles. After fixing it, 49%; after fixing five gap-filling problems, 90%. Sites whose terms prohibit automated fetching were not imported.

item.title: Four gaps in monitoring X: posts missing from search, accounts that change hands, a store-finding query, and catching up after an outage
item.description: Four stores’ lottery posts did not appear in search even after 751 posts; a registered store had become a person; store-finding found 11 of 63; and after a 6-day outage only 185 of 2,866 were read in 2 hours. Fixes and cost estimates.

item.title: When you cannot watch everything quickly: popular 128 of 427 sets run fast, and the fastest lane yields to the budget
item.description: Full laps over 427 sets took 4 to 24 hours. A separate lane for 128 popular sets and truly once-a-minute checks for popular items; batching stopped another monitor and measuring over a short window misjudged cost.

item.title: Fixing a gate does not fix existing data: a “tried already” mark, a URL marker and a lookup table
item.description: After fixing a judgement, 12 of 32 existing articles stayed wrong (the skip mark lasts 7 days); a marker stored in the URL was lost on link rewrite and 111 articles were split again; removing a table key left written values. Five reports had one shape.

item.title: Fixing product genre from the official catalogue: three dry runs took 13 changes down to 4
item.description: A Duel Masters product was registered as Pokémon. Making the official catalogue the source of truth, my first dry run would have moved nine correct Weiss Schwarz products to another game; after three dry runs there were 0 misfires.

item.title: 393 “work-name-only” products from an official list: the name field did not contain the product form
item.description: An official-list import created 502 products in one day (usually 1–10). The name field held only the work name; the form was in the category. Cleaning 393 and re-registering 328 correct names took alias collisions from 0 pairs to 250.

item.title: Online play that trusts nothing the client says: the server decides moves, clocks and results
item.description: Online play without login. Moves are validated by the rules engine, the clock lives only on the server, a disconnect gets 30 seconds, tokens are signed with HMAC, and ratings use pre-match numbers. With real values from the server code.

item.title: “The same application page” does not mean “the same store”: 52 articles showed another store’s name
item.description: A job that unified store names across articles sharing an application page turned a Sendai store into “Shinjuku South Exit”. One page was shared by 15 separate stores. I changed it to unify only when confirmed the same place and restored 52 articles from an untouched field.

item.title: When first-come sales start, the site becomes a waiting-room page: a 15 KB notice slipped through an 8,000-byte gate
item.description: On AEON Style Online, a first-come sale turned the whole site into a 15 KB “heavy access” page. It passed the 8,000-byte check added earlier that day and was read as “success, 0 products”. I switched to a title check; Amazon’s 13 minutes were serial AI screening.

item.title: Before widening concurrency slots: widening a 2-core server from 8 to 14, and the earlier conclusion that was half wrong
item.description: Shortening intervals made the 1-minute first-come monitor wait for a slot. I widened slots from 8 to 11 and 14 and measured. The real cap was not CPU but jobs sleeping on Rakuten API’s 1.5-second wait while holding slots.

item.title: Three mix-ups in splitting one article into products: a child treated as a parent, a shared link pointing to another store, a name owned by two products
item.description: Reprocessing a split “child” hid 60 lotteries closing that day (23 stores); a link-only lookup shared by 13 stores picked another store’s parent; names claimed by two products numbered 267 pairs. Real items vanished with nothing on screen.

item.title: Four times my own tools hurt me: a summary dropped conditions, one undefined stopped saving, a check locked out production, alerts that never cleared
item.description: A “15 characters” prompt dropped entry conditions in 671 checked lotteries; one undefined broke every save and burned 41% of a day’s credits; six parallel requests got the production IP blocked; I made alerts that kept ringing after the fix.

item.title: Every deploy re-ran the daily jobs: 477 runs in 48 hours, 46.6% of that day’s Gemini cost
item.description: A once-a-day job ran 43 times and used 46.6% of a day’s Gemini cost. Timed-out runs never wrote their last-run time, so every restart treated them as missed. A deploy at 08:00 also swallowed the digest.

item.title: Notifications cannot be recalled: 19% of the last 72 hours’ notifications were wrong, and the gate worked after the fact
item.description: Of 644 notifications in 72 hours, 122 (19%) were wrong. The article gate hides articles later, but a notification goes out about 0.6 seconds after saving; 25 of 30 hidden articles had already been pushed. I put the same gate at the notification entrance.

item.title: A “1-minute” monitor checked each item once per 10 minutes: before speeding up, count the revisit interval and what was delivered
item.description: A first-come monitor watched 63 items but checked 4–9 per run, so each item once per 10 minutes, and caught 3 sales in 7 days. Shortening other intervals slowed it further, and “not screened” meant 45% of first-come listings got no notification.

item.title: Four real lotteries silently thrown away: a regex, dates without a year, batched answers and null
item.description: “x.com” matched “e-starbox.com” so application links were never used; a date with no year was read as 2020 so no Pokémon items were imported; batched answers got out of step; “cannot decide” was read as “none” and nearly hid 129 lotteries.

item.title: “Checked” marks on articles that had never been read: the t.co relay page
item.description: Opened with a browser User-Agent, t.co returned a relay page instead of redirecting. All 220 displayed articles were unread and 9 were closed forms. How I fixed it and how I removed the wrong “checked” marks.

item.title: Before cutting Gemini cost, I doubted the meter: price, breakdown and cache were all wrong, and the cache threshold changed when I re-measured
item.description: The cost meter was broken in three places (prices under-reported 2.6×, 31 purposes merged, cache uncounted). The cache threshold was about 8,000 tokens in September and about 4,000 in October. Padding the prompt shifted 9% of answers.

item.title: Firestore cost in yen: 91% of reads came from one place, and my first cache did not work
item.description: Seen in yen for the first time, Firestore cost about ¥13,000 a month, close to Gemini. 91% of reads were a product list re-read for every post. A 60-second cache failed because 32 jobs ran at once; caching the pending promise fixed it.

item.title: Setting the rules of Negaeri Shogi by playing AI against AI: one change that worked, six that broke
item.description: A 6×6 board game where sandwiched pieces defect. Instead of guessing the numbers, I ran 40 to 100 AI-vs-AI games per rule. Flips per move went from 2% to 81%, removing the king guard ended games in 17 moves, and the first-move edge is still unsolved.

item.title: Pokémon card sleeves and loaders: sizes and what “pt” means
item.description: What to check before buying Pokémon card sleeves, toploaders and deck boxes: standard vs small size, what 35pt means, and a buying checklist. Not a hands-on review; unverified points are listed.

item.title: ITMS-91064 “Invalid Binary”: NSPrivacyTracking was true but NSPrivacyTrackingDomains was empty
item.description: An iOS build was rejected by Apple's automated review with ITMS-91064. NSPrivacyTracking was true while NSPrivacyTrackingDomains was an empty array. How it was fixed, and what was not verified.

item.title: App Store review sent “Guideline 2.1 Information Needed”: the six things Apple asked for
item.description: My first App Store submission got a request for more information (Guideline 2.1), not a rejection. The six things Apple asked for and how they connect to earlier fixes.

item.title: Firebase 12 does not work with Xcode 15.2 (Swift 6.0 required): why I pinned Firebase 11.4.0 and AdMob 11.5.0
item.description: On an old Mac stuck on Xcode 15.2, newer Firebase and AdMob SDKs fail to build. Which versions break, which I pinned (Firebase 11.4.0, AdMob 11.5.0), and why.

item.title: iOS app freezes and is killed (0x8BADF00D): a SwiftUI computed property ran on every redraw
item.description: An iOS app was force-quit by the watchdog (0x8BADF00D). A SwiftUI computed property re-filtered and re-sorted 951 articles on the main thread every body evaluation.

item.title: No builds arriving in TestFlight: I had used up the 25 free Xcode Cloud hours (my first diagnosis was wrong)
item.description: New builds stopped appearing in TestFlight. My first diagnosis (“[ci skip] is blocking builds”) was wrong; the workflow built the iOS app on every commit.
